_comment: Machine-readable Robotaxied Constitution. Every consequential action taken by the vehicle, a remote operator, or an emergency authority is checked against this before it is authorized. This is deliberately a plain, hand-editable policy document, not a trained model -- the whole point is that a denial (or a conflict resolution) can be traced to a specific line here.
_authority_hierarchy_comment: Lower index = higher priority when two independently-authorized actions conflict over the same decision point. This ordering is a policy choice, not a law of nature -- it's configurable here, not hard-coded in firewall.py, precisely so it can be argued about and changed.
_passenger_comment: The passenger is a real actor in this model, not just a one-time input at trip start -- they set the original intent envelope, but they can also issue live requests mid-trip, and those requests outrank the vehicle's own operational authority and the remote operator's, per authority_hierarchy. This is the tier most robotaxi discourse skips: how much authority did the passenger actually keep after saying 'take me to the airport'?
_emergency_data_share_comment: request_data_share is deliberately a REQUEST, not a command: emergency_authority_may_not includes disable_vehicle_safety_systems and there is no compel_data_share action anywhere in this file. Police can ask a remote operator to share telemetry; nothing in this constitution lets them take it by commanding the vehicle directly. That distinction -- may request vs. may compel -- is the whole point of listing this as an emergency_authority_may item rather than baking it into command_stop or override_route.
_emergency_authority_comment: An emergency responder (police, fire, EMS acting under defined emergency protocol) outranks a remote operator and the vehicle's own operational authority -- but still cannot override an immutable constraint. Nobody can.
